stories.title: Uruguay signs multi billion dollar deal for 500 MW data center park
stories.summary: Uruguay has signed a US$ 5.7 billion agreement with Spanish company Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente (Solaria) to develop a 500 MW data center technology park powered partly by its own solar generation, in what the government describes as the largest investment in the country’s history. President Yamandú Orsi signed the agreement on Wednesday, October […]
stories.content:
Uruguay has signed a US$ 5.7 billion agreement with Spanish company Solaria Energía y Medio Ambiente (Solaria) to develop a 500 MW data center technology park powered partly by its own solar generation, in what the government describes as the largest investment in the country’s history.

President Yamandú Orsi signed the agreement on Wednesday, October 14 and the project will operate under Uruguay’s free zone regime and involve US$ 5.5 billion in data center infrastructure and US$ 200 million in solar energy facilities.

According to a press release, the development will take place in two phases across Canelones, San José and Florida. The first phase will include 200 MW of data center capacity and 350 MW of solar generation, while the second will add another 300 MW of data center capacity, with the possibility of expanding solar production.

Fernanda Cardona, Minister, Ministry of Industry Energy and Mining (MIEM), Uruguay, described the agreement as a “historic investment” and said, “We are signing it in this administration, but it will continue to be deployed in the administration that comes, in the interior of the country, regardless of who is there, this transcends” governments and “we are leaving a work commitment” that “will have a spillover in this five-year period and the next”, she added, describing the development as “a country project”.

Cardona also credited coordination between government ministries, public companies and diplomatic representatives in Spain for securing the agreement, describing the negotiations as a “silent, forceful and record-breaking” effort that “closed in less than five months”.

The project is expected to benefit information technology, data center operations and maintenance, solar power generation and electricity grid services for existing facilities such as Antel’s data center in Pando, its planned facility in Canelones and Google’s data center. Uruguay’s electricity infrastructure, submarine cables, renewable energy capacity and political stability as factors attracting investment to establish Uruguay as a digital hub.

Solaria has operated in Uruguay for nearly a decade, with solar power plants in Young, Río Negro department, and Mercedes, Soriano department, which supply electricity to state-owned utility UTE. Founded in Spain in 2002, the company develops and operates photovoltaic energy projects. It has been listed on the Spanish stock exchange since 2007 and joined the IBEX 35 index in 2020.

stories.title: Memphis council delays data center moratorium vote again
stories.summary: The Memphis City Council has again postponed a vote on a proposed 12-month data center moratorium. This delay allows officials to assess social, health, and environmental impacts of data centers.
stories.content:
The Memphis City Council has delayed a vote on a proposed 12-month data center moratorium for a second time.Councilors voted 7-5 to postpone the decision, with a new vote now expected on October 20. The moratorium, proposed by councilor JB Smiley Jr., would allow officials to assess data centers’ social, health, and environmental impacts. More than 100 residents reportedly protested the delay.Similar restrictions are under consideration across the US amid growing opposition to AI and data center development. Memphis hosts several facilities operated by xAI, rebranded as SpaceXAI, which power Grok and provide cloud services to clients including Anthropic.These xAI sites face lawsuits over alleged gas turbine permit violations. Councilor Jeff Warren warned that a moratorium could divert investment to neighboring Mississippi counties like DeSoto, Crittenden, Fayette, and Tipton. An xAI facility in Mississippi would remain unaffected by a Memphis moratorium.

stories.summary: Malaysia has approved 27 data center projects with an estimated investment of RM225.97 billion (US$ 55.4 billion) as of July 2026, the Digital Ministry informed Parliament yesterday. It added that all are still under construction except for one which has started operations without specifying its location. More than half (16) of the data centers which were approved by […]
stories.content:
Malaysia has approved 27 data center projects with an estimated investment of RM225.97 billion (US$ 55.4 billion) as of July 2026, the Digital Ministry informed Parliament yesterday.

It added that all are still under construction except for one which has started operations without specifying its location. More than half (16) of the data centers which were approved by the data centre task force (DCTF) are located in Johor. This is followed by Selangor (10) and Negeri Sembilan (1).

The projects are expected to create 4,053 jobs, including 3,523 high-skilled positions in electrical and mechanical engineering, networking, cybersecurity, as well as data center operations and maintenance. About 90 per cent of the high-skilled positions are expected to be taken up by Malaysians.

The ministry said the projects are subject to a minimum local content requirement of 30 per cent, with implementation and compliance monitored by the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) through project implementation reports that must be submitted every six months.

Talent Corporation Malaysia is in the midst of developing a data center facilities management programme to train locals in data center operations and maintenance, the ministry added.

Also in Parliament recently, it was revealed that as of August, 45 operational facilities had a combined maximum load of 6GW but consumed about 1.37GW. As a result, Deputy Minister Abdul Rahman Mohamad proposed that operators consider developing their own power generation and water supply arrangements.

In other news, in response to the power constraints in Johor, a planned 1GW hybrid energy project by UEM Lestra could strengthen Johor’s electricity supply and reduce dependence on other states. An expert told a local paper that generation nearer to major data center clusters could reduce transmission losses and improve supply resilience.

stories.title: Princeton Digital Group seeks US$1.2 billion loan to fund Johor data center: Report
stories.summary: Singapore-headquartered data center operator Princeton Digital Group Ltd (PDG) is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion (RM4.9 billion) to fund its Johor data center buildout amid its Asian expansion, Bloomberg reported yesterday citing people familiar with the matter. The three-year loan will be arranged by HSBC Holdings plc Singapore branch, Maybank Investment […]
stories.content:
Singapore-headquartered data center operator Princeton Digital Group Ltd (PDG) is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion (RM4.9 billion) to fund its Johor data center buildout amid its Asian expansion, Bloomberg reported yesterday citing people familiar with the matter.

The three-year loan will be arranged by HSBC Holdings plc Singapore branch, Maybank Investment Bank Bhd, OCBC Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore) Ltd, and United Overseas Bank Ltd.

The proceeds will be used to fund its 198.8-MW data center campus in Johor, Malaysia and to refinance existing debt, said the people, adding that PDG’s subsidiary Princeton Digital Group Labuan Alpha Ltd, will be taking up the loan.

Representatives for Princeton Digital Group, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC Malaysia and UOB didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment while Standard Chartered declined to comment.

In May, PDG announced it raised about US$856 million for its Indonesian data center buildout. It is targetting to raise US$5 billion in debt to support its regional expansion plans, as announced earlier this year.

PDG’s investors include Warburg Pincus (its top shareholder), Stonepeak Partners, Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala Investment Co and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board.

The firm operates more than 1.8GW of data center capacity across Asia including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia.

stories.title: AI pushes data center cooling limits; smart systems crucial
stories.summary: AI workloads are driving data center rack power densities past 100 kW, with some clusters nearing 1 megawatt. This necessitates more intelligent cooling solutions to maintain uptime and energy efficiency.
stories.content:
AI workloads are significantly increasing the thermal demands on data centres, pushing rack power beyond 100 kW, with some AI clusters projected to exceed 1 megawatt in the coming years.Operators must deploy AI capacity rapidly while safeguarding uptime, managing energy consumption, and protecting valuable hardware. The optimal cooling architecture depends on factors such as rack power, workload type, and facility specifications.Advanced liquid cooling is typically reserved for AI racks, while other methods serve standard workloads and facilities without existing water infrastructure. This blend of cooling approaches introduces complexities, including mitigating leak risks, supporting multiple architectures simultaneously, and ensuring precise thermal response.Moving heat more efficiently is no longer sufficient. Cooling systems need greater intelligence through real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management. These technologies can enhance responsiveness, reduce energy consumption, and maximise uptime, while also establishing a basis for AI-enabled predictive maintenance.
### Smarter Control and Sensing

Consider a leak in a liquid-cooled rack. Many current installations use on-off valves that halt coolant flow upon leak detection, shutting down the entire rack until repairs are made. Resistive ropes, common leak sensors, can be limited in accuracy and response time.A more intelligent system could detect leaks faster and control coolant flow at the server-tray level, allowing unaffected parts of the rack to continue operating. This approach combines real-time motor control, precision flow sensing, and high-efficiency power management.Within the coolant distribution unit (CDU), pumps and fans are critical for the cooling loop's stability. Real-time motor control helps maintain system stability, with microcontrollers processing sensor data to adjust performance, and motor drivers operating pumps and fans efficiently. Motor control also extends to the server tray, where linear valves can regulate coolant flow more precisely as power density increases.Precise flow control requires accurate flow measurement, so linear valves at the tray level work with flow sensors to enable granular control of GPU and CPU die temperatures. Non-invasive ultrasonic sensing can avoid creating additional leak points and simplify installation. Alternative leak detection methods, such as humidity sensors, capacitive sensors, and negative-pressure CDU designs, are being evaluated due to concerns about the accuracy and response time of resistive ropes. Flow readings, combined with data from temperature, humidity, and pressure sensors, contribute to a comprehensive operational overview.
### Efficient Power Management and Edge AI

The pumps and fans used to cool AI racks consume power, making their efficiency crucial. Gallium nitride (GaN) power devices in pump drives can improve overall pump-system efficiency by up to 2 per cent compared with traditional silicon, also allowing for a smaller form factor. Fans in server trays, which often combine air and liquid cooling, are shifting from 12 V to 48 V to reduce power consumption. Power delivery is also evolving, with CDU pumps supporting input voltages from 48 V DC to 380 V AC, and future designs needing to support 800 V high-voltage DC (HVDC) distribution.Sensing capabilities can also become predictive. Edge AI can process data from a cooling system’s full sensor array through “sensor fusion,” leading to faster response times and lower latency. This improves leak detection speed and accuracy, addressing a key bottleneck for reliable liquid cooling. Sensor fusion also enables predictive maintenance for pumps and other mechanical components. Combined with tray-level flow control, edge AI and sensor fusion point towards cooling systems that sense conditions, anticipate problems, and adjust autonomously.No single cooling design suits every AI data centre, and mixed architectures are expected to remain prevalent. However, all architectures share common building blocks: sensors for measurement, motor control for pumps, fans, and valves, efficient power management, and processors for system coordination. The benefits emerge when these components function as an integrated system. Data centres that can keep pace with increasing AI computing densities will be those equipped with intelligent and resilient cooling systems.

stories.title: Brazil data center growth moves beyond São Paulo
stories.summary: Brazil's data center market is expanding beyond São Paulo to new hubs like Rio de Janeiro and Fortaleza, driven by hyperscale and AI projects. New federal tax incentives could improve project economics outside the traditional base. However, power availability and environmental permitting remain key constraints for new capacity delivery.
stories.content:
Brazil’s data center market is expanding beyond its traditional hub in São Paulo to include Rio de Janeiro, Fortaleza, and southern Brazil, according to DC Byte’s August market analysis. This shift is driven by increasing hyperscale cloud demand and emerging AI-driven projects. São Paulo currently holds 76 per cent of Brazil’s live data center capacity, benefiting from its high customer concentration and dense network connectivity.However, São Paulo faces challenges with a dwindling supply of powered land and slow transmission grid upgrades. This situation pushes developers to explore new regions, even as these areas present their own infrastructure hurdles. New federal tax incentives, enacted under the ReData framework, could improve project economics in other parts of the country.
### Key development challenges

Power availability remains a central factor in the speed of new capacity delivery. While Brazil has access to renewable electricity, connecting sites to the grid on schedule poses a significant challenge.Rodrigo Gomez, a senior Latin America analyst at DC Byte, noted that the pace of electrical infrastructure development is the market’s main constraint. Bruno Porto, manager for industrial, logistics, and data centers in Brazil at JLL, added that some locations require transmission reinforcement before supporting additional data center load. Environmental licensing in Brazil is also critical, potentially taking up to 18 months depending on the project’s region and scale, Porto said.
### Regional market dynamics

Outside São Paulo, emerging markets offer varied advantages. Rio de Janeiro is positioned as a gateway for digital services in eastern Brazil, with planned capacity including Rio AI City targeting approximately 3 GW. Fortaleza leverages its extensive network of submarine cable landings, strengthening its role as a connectivity hub for the Americas and Africa.Southern Brazil, particularly Rio Grande do Sul, provides access to neighboring Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay. This creates potential for supporting cloud, telecommunications, and digital infrastructure across the Southern Cone. These regional developments reflect Brazil’s evolution from a domestic market into a broader connectivity platform, Gomez stated.
### Impact of tax incentives

Brazil’s ReData framework, signed into law by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on September 15, provides federal tax relief for qualifying technology equipment. This includes import-duty relief for equipment without a domestic equivalent.The framework aims to encourage regional diversification by reducing certain obligations for investments in the North, Northeast, and Central-West regions. Porto commented that these fiscal changes improve Brazil’s competitiveness regarding capital expenditure for new data center installations. Despite these incentives, the pace of grid reinforcement and environmental approvals will ultimately determine when new facilities can serve customers.

stories.title: US AI data centre land buying hits $6 billion; power access drives premiums
stories.summary: US land purchases for future data centres reached approximately $6 billion in the first half of 2026, marking a 79 per cent increase year-over-year. This surge is driven by demand for large AI campuses, with power access becoming a more significant factor in land valuation than location alone.
stories.content:
US purchases of land for future data centres reached about $6 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Avison Young. This figure represents a 79 per cent increase from a year earlier. The spending reflects strong demand for large AI campuses, as hyperscalers, neocloud providers, energy-first developers and investors compete to secure sites for new computing capacity.For data centre operators, the stakes are both operational and financial. Delayed power can push back capacity delivery and complicate customer commitments. It can also leave expensive buildings waiting to enter service.
### Power Access Drives Valuation

"The biggest thing right now is speed to power," John Andril, manager of market intelligence at Avison Young, told TechTarget. In Northern Virginia, entitled land without power can sell for roughly $4 million an acre. Powered land in the same region commands at least $6 million an acre, Andril said. Entitlements, infrastructure and other site characteristics also affect prices.An Altus Group analysis of 80 verified data centre land transactions in August found committed utility load was the strongest predictor of land pricing. Sites associated with 230-kilovolt or 500-kV infrastructure traded at approximately 2.4 times the pricing of sites with 138-kV or lower infrastructure. Transmission access can reduce required project upgrades. Existing infrastructure can also shorten the regulatory process by about a year, Andril said. However, proximity to a transmission line does not guarantee timely delivery of required capacity."The premium is increasingly payment for uncertainty removed, not just for megawatts nearby," said Neil Osnato, an industry analyst. A genuinely power-ready property typically needs electrical infrastructure deliverable within about 18 months. This timeframe roughly matches the time needed to prepare a building for its initial load, Andril said. Developers also require clarity on substation equipment and its funding and construction. For campus planning, developers generally use about 0.5 to 1 acre per megawatt as a rule of thumb.
### Developer and Utility Challenges

Utilities face a planning problem. They must prepare for large new loads without spending billions on projects that may not materialise. Developers seek confidence in power delivery before committing substantial capital to a site. Andril described this as a "chicken-and-egg" situation.Letters of credit, take-or-pay agreements and stricter interconnection-queue requirements can help utilities differentiate serious projects from speculative requests. Established developers and end users can support these measures. Removing speculative projects makes legitimate demand easier to evaluate, Andril said. Onsite generation offers another option to support initial operations while waiting for utility infrastructure. The financial viability of this approach depends on generation costs and project economics.

stories.title: Why tech, data centre IPOs are facing delays – and what investors can expect of the market now
stories.summary: Market volatility and rising interest rates are some reasons for the pause on listings

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
Market volatility and rising interest rates are some reasons for the pause on listings

\[SINGAPORE\] Major tech, artificial intelligence and data centre companies have put the brakes on their initial public offering plans since September, citing uncertain market conditions.

This includes the proposed listing of Blackstone-backed Airtrunk’s Singapore real estate investment trust (Reit), which could have raised US$1.5 billion, and Australia-based data centre operator Firmus’ potential IPO, which was withdrawn in October.

AI giant OpenAI is another player which has delayed its listing, with founder and CEO Sam Altman saying it will not go public in 2026 amid AI safety concerns.

So why have these IPOs been paused now, and what can investors expect moving forward? *The Business Times* spoke to experts to find out more.

## Rising interest rate woes

Companies are delaying or shelving listing plans altogether because interest rates have risen significantly in the past month, analysts told BT.

Borrowing costs have risen since the US Federal Reserve hiked rates by 25 basis points on Sep 16 to a range of 3.75 to 4 per cent.

This makes fund raising via equity or bonds more difficult for companies.

Data-centre Reits that pay dividends, in particular, are affected as they must refinance any debt at higher interest rates. This will impact yield as dividends are squeezed by loan repayments.

Reits’ dividends will struggle to outpace rising long yields of government bonds, said Nirgunan Tiruchelvam, head of consumer and Internet research at Aletheia Capital.

In this hawkish environment, asset managers may re-allocate capital away from dividend-paying counters such as Reits into US Treasuries or high-grade corporate bonds.

This puts AirTrunk’s proposed Singapore data centre listing in a bind, said Tiruchelvam.

Reits in Singapore have felt the impact of a higher interest-rate environment, as the benchmark iEdge S-Reit Index has fallen 12 per cent year to date while bond yields escalate.

## An overcrowded space

At present there are a number of AI-related projects seeking funding, which is leading to an overcrowded market.

“Companies late to the IPO game are now thinking twice about listing and getting lower subscription (levels),” said Francis Tan, chief strategist, Asia, at Indosuez Wealth Management.

Firmus sought to raise US$5 billion for its IPO on the Australian Securities Exchange. This would have valued the company at US$30.6 billion, nearly triple the US$10.5 billion valuation after its August funding round – an “extravagant price” to experts.

The company would go on to scrap its IPO plans after investors pulled out, with media reports of Firmus seeking private funding instead.

Other companies which have shelved public listings recently include advanced materials manufacturer Amaero and smart ring maker Oura. Both were slated to list in the US in September.

Market uncertainty was a reason for Oura’s IPO delay. It could have been valued as much as US$15 billion, as it sought to raise US$2.2 billion.

IPO underwriters may hesitate amid a volatile market due to risks of undersubscription, and how a strong listing debut is uncertain, said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research, Asia at Morningstar.

She added: “Pulled IPOs...reflect weakness in investor sentiment so companies may not get the pricing they want in the IPO.”

But this is not a sign of the broader AI trade wobbling, said Tiruchelvam.

“The AI trade is becoming more discerning (now). The market now separates those who earn from AI from those who spend on it.”

This is evident within the data-centre space, as traditional data centres firms see their spreads widen, signalling risks. However hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon and Meta have seen the reverse, with their spreads tightening as investors seek less risk.

Some are pushing ahead, however, like Singapore-headquartered data centre operator DayOne.

## Not all doom and gloom

DayOne’s revenue more than tripled to US$512 million in the first half of this year, while raising over US$6 billion in equity since 2024 – with no sign of any “forced selling” qualities.

This is “a better story told at a dangerous moment”, amid a data-centre operator listing freeze, said Tiruchelvam.

But he notes the company’s US$20 billion valuation is roughly 20 times annualised sales of US$1 billion based on its Nasdaq IPO filing, with losses widening, too.

Net losses stood at US$81.9 million for the six months ended Jun 30, surging from US$13.5 million a year prior.

“I expect a valuation haircut, not a retreat,” said Tiruchelvam. “But if yields keep climbing, it may join AirTrunk in the 2027 (IPO) queue.”

DayOne officially filed for a US Nasdaq IPO directly in October this year, citing plans to raise as much as US$5 billion.

Previously the company considered a dual listing via the Singapore Exchange’s (SGX) Global Listing Board, though it was not mentioned in the prospectus.

BT understands that a subsequent listing on the SGX has not been ruled out.

stories.title: ASML warns of AI chipmaking tool supply shortfall
stories.summary: ASML Holding NV warned that its chip-making machines face a potential supply shortfall in the next two years. This is due to soaring artificial intelligence spending, which could impact data center and AI infrastructure development.
stories.content:
ASML Holding NV has warned of a potential supply shortfall for its chip-making machines in 2027 and 2028.The company stated that its current supply plans cannot fully meet demand, even as it increased its 2026 sales forecast. Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said that customers are requesting more tools daily. ASML is exploring options to boost capacity for 2028 beyond the previously announced 30 per cent increase.The Veldhoven, Netherlands-based company projects annual sales between €44 billion and €45 billion for this year. This is an increase from its earlier low-end forecast of €43 billion. ASML is the sole manufacturer of cutting-edge lithography machines essential for producing semiconductors that power the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.The company's outlook provides insight into the investment plans of major chipmakers. These include Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., Samsung Electronics Co., and Intel Corp., as spending on AI infrastructure continues to surge. Some customers are also showing interest in placing orders for 2029 and 2030.ASML is working to accelerate tool shipments by reducing the cycle time from production to delivery. It has also started constructing its second industrial campus in the Netherlands, with the first phase expected to be completed in 2029. South Korea was ASML's largest market for new system tools in the third quarter, followed by Taiwan and China.

stories.title: Global data centre power incidents rising, UK second highest
stories.summary: The UK ranks second globally for reported data centre fires and electrical incidents, behind the United States, according to the Energy Incident Register. Worldwide, 92 incidents were recorded between 2010 and October 2026, with a noticeable increase in recent years.
stories.content:
The UK ranks second globally for reported data centre fires and electrical incidents, trailing only the United States, according to the Energy Incident Register. This register has compiled 92 incidents involving data centre power infrastructure worldwide between 2010 and October 2026.Of these incidents, 52 involved fires or thermal events, and 17 were classified as major. The global trend indicates a rise in incidents, with eight reported in 2024, 20 in 2025, and 18 recorded so far in 2026. The United States accounts for the largest share with 33 incidents, followed by the UK with 14. India and France each recorded five incidents.Despite the UK's high ranking, only two of its 14 recorded incidents occurred from 2024 onwards. One was in 2024, and another in 2026. The most recent UK incident involved a fire in a Blackwall, east London data centre in January 2026, caused by a lead-acid battery failure. A May 2024 power failure at a privately operated data centre for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) disrupted government digital services for 85 hours.The Energy Incident Register's methodology, which retrospectively assembled historical data, cautions against interpreting rising historical counts as declining safety. The Uptime Institute's Annual Outage Analysis 2026 found that outage frequency per site declined for the fifth consecutive year. However, it noted that the pace of improvement was slowing.UPS systems and battery rooms are the most frequently identified equipment in these incidents, featuring in 22 cases. Backup generators appeared in 15 incidents, while switchgear and electrical rooms were involved in 10. Uptime Institute's research also identifies power as the leading cause of impactful outages, with UPS systems, transfer switches, and generators being principal failure points.

stories.title: India to roll out data centre policy amid power use concerns
stories.summary: India will introduce a dedicated policy for data centres, a minister said on Wednesday. This move follows public protests in cities like Mumbai and Visakhapatnam against planned facilities by Amazon and Google, citing water and electricity usage concerns.
stories.content:
India plans to implement a dedicated data centre policy to prevent consumers from facing higher electricity costs due to the sector's power consumption, a junior IT minister stated on Wednesday.The policy initiative comes after protests by residents in Mumbai and Visakhapatnam against data centres proposed by Amazon and Google. These protests highlighted concerns regarding water and electricity usage, as well as noise.Currently, India approves data centres under existing environmental and building regulations. Some states also offer specific incentives for the sector.Junior IT minister Jitin Prasada, who made the announcement, did not provide details on the policy's scope or its unveiling timeline. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government views the data centre sector as a significant $200 billion opportunity.Prasada stated at a New Delhi event, organised by the Central Electricity Authority, that India offers a "very fertile ground for hyperscale data centres." He noted that data centres in certain countries were diverting power from consumers, leading to increased electricity prices, a situation India aims to avoid.Amazon and Google have denied any wrongdoing. They maintain that their facilities use advanced technologies to minimise resource consumption, making the concerns unfounded.

CtrlS Datacenters Ltd will invest ₹10,000 crore in Bihar to construct a 150 MW hyperscale artificial intelligence (AI) facility in Bodh Gaya. stories.title: Hyundai & Kia back VAST Data in strategic investment
stories.summary: The investment follows years of production use and has already helped 42dot halve storage needs while keeping autonomous driving work within existing data centre capacity.
stories.content:
Hyundai Motor and Kia have made a strategic investment in VAST Data, extending an existing relationship focused on software and data systems for autonomous driving and robotics.

Their autonomous mobility division, 42dot, has already been using VAST's platform in production for advanced driver assistance systems research and autonomous driving workloads. The investment follows several years of operational use, during which 42dot moved those workloads onto a single data platform built with NVIDIA infrastructure.

That consolidation brought advanced driver assistance systems and large language model development together on one platform after they had previously been spread across different vendor systems. The companies said the shift halved storage needs and enabled 42dot to expand within its existing data centre footprint instead of building or leasing more capacity.

The deal gives VAST another strategic backer following its Series F fundraising, which valued the company at USD $30 billion. Existing investors in that round included NVIDIA, Fidelity Management & Research Company, and NEA.

### Data demands

The investment reflects growing pressure on carmakers to manage the data generated by autonomous vehicle development. A single sensor-equipped test vehicle can produce terabytes of information each day from cameras, LiDAR, radar, and ultrasonic sensors, and that volume rises sharply across larger fleets.

Those workloads also place different demands on the same infrastructure. Raw sensor data, video clips, model validation, software update synchronisation, and telematics each require different levels of throughput, latency, and oversight.

VAST's role in Hyundai Motor and Kia's software stack sits within 42dot, the group's autonomous mobility and software unit. Its systems run on NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD infrastructure using NVIDIA Hopper, with VAST providing the data layer for research and development.

VAST also supports data replication across 42dot's data centre sites and allows simulation, training, and validation pipelines to operate from the same namespace without copies, according to the companies. The approach is intended to reduce duplication as artificial intelligence projects scale.

Executive Vice President Hokeun Chung of HKMC's Future Strategy Division said the investment followed direct operational experience with the system.

"Our journey with VAST started as a customer," said Chung. "Consolidating our ADAS and language model development onto one platform changed how quickly our teams can move from data collection to a validated model. Our work in autonomous driving and robotics depends on being able to use the data our vehicles generate quickly and reliably, and as data volumes grow it requires infrastructure that can keep pace. This investment reflects our confidence, earned in production, that VAST is the right long-term partner for that scale."

### From customer to investor

The move from user to investor is notable in a market where automotive groups are increasingly taking stakes in suppliers whose tools underpin artificial intelligence development. For VAST, it also provides a reference customer in one of the most data-intensive industrial uses of AI, where software training depends on fast access to large volumes of sensor and video data.

Hyundai Motor and Kia have been expanding their software and robotics work as carmakers seek to control more of the technology stack behind assisted and autonomous driving. Data management has become central to that effort because fragmented storage systems can slow development and create duplication across engineering teams.

VAST argues that older high-performance computing storage systems can become a bottleneck when large fleets of AI processors are waiting for data. Its architecture is designed to keep those processors supplied without splitting data across multiple storage environments.

Renen Hallak, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of VAST Data, linked the investment to broader changes in industrial AI.

"The companies building physical AI such as vehicles, robots and machines, are running into the same data problem enterprises hit years ago, and at a much larger scale. We remain committed to breaking decades-old trade-offs to deliver the data infrastructure stack for AI. HKMC's decision to invest in VAST, having already seen the benefits of our technology, shows that our infrastructure is core to their future and capable of meeting the increasing needs of AI," said Hallak.

stories.title: TBH appoints Brittany Lam as director in Singapore
stories.summary: As data centre and infrastructure investment surges across Asia, TBH is bolstering its advisory team to help clients assess project risk and readiness.
stories.content:
Thu, 15th Oct 2026 (Today)
TBH has appointed Brittany Lam as a Director in its Asia team, based in Singapore.

Lam will work across the firm's Strategic Advisory practice in the region, focusing on supporting investors, lenders and developers with transaction advisory, technical due diligence and major capital investment decisions.

Her appointment comes as investment in data centres, energy projects and industrial infrastructure continues across Asia, driving demand for independent technical and commercial advice on project readiness and risks that could affect returns and delivery.

Lam brings more than 16 years of experience across investment, consulting and technical advisory. Her work has covered data centres, renewable energy, water, critical minerals and major industrial developments, as well as advisory work for public and private sector organisations.

Before joining TBH, she advised investors, lenders and developers in Asia and other markets on acquisitions and financing processes, including more than 2GW of hyperscale data centre projects.

### Regional demand

TBH has built a strategic advisory presence around large capital projects, combining technical and commercial analysis with its work in planning, cost, risk and project delivery. Lam's background in lenders' technical advisory and technical due diligence will strengthen its support for clients from early-stage investment decisions through to financial close and delivery.

Her Singapore-based appointment also reflects the importance of South East Asia as a hub for project finance, infrastructure development and cross-border investment. Demand for data centre capacity has risen across several Asian markets as cloud providers, digital platforms and enterprise customers expand their regional operations, while energy and industrial projects continue to attract institutional and strategic capital.

Since 2010, TBH has worked on more than 100 hyperscale data centre projects across the Asia-Pacific region. This activity forms part of a broader consultancy business established in Australia in 1965, with operations spanning Oceania, Asia and the Middle East.

Stuart Cassie, Partner & Global Advisory Lead at TBH, said the appointment reflected changing client needs in Asia's infrastructure and digital asset markets.

"Asia is seeing significant investment across data centres, energy and other major infrastructure. Clients increasingly need independent advice that brings together the commercial and technical realities of those investments," said Stuart Cassie, Partner & Global Advisory Lead, TBH.

He added that Lam's mix of finance, technical advisory and delivery experience would deepen the firm's regional and international advisory bench.

"Brittany has advised on some of the region's most significant transactions and brings a rare combination of finance, technical advisory and project delivery experience. Her appointment strengthens our Strategic Advisory capability in Asia and globally, and further enhances our ability to support investors, lenders and developers from the earliest stages of due diligence right through to construction and operations," Cassie said.

Lam's experience spans both the commercial assessment of investments and the practical issues tied to project execution. This includes identifying risks that may affect financing, testing whether projects are ready to proceed and assessing technical factors that can influence delivery outcomes.

For firms involved in infrastructure and digital assets, these questions have become more prominent as projects grow in scale and complexity. Lenders and investors also face greater scrutiny over timelines, construction assumptions, supply chain exposure and operational readiness before committing capital.

Lam will help clients navigate these issues across transactions and delivery decisions in Asia, where demand for specialist advice has increased alongside investment volumes.

stories.title: DigiCo secures 71MW Sydney data centre contract as it prioritises Australia
stories.summary: DigiCo Infrastructure REIT has signed a 15-year contract for 71MW of data centre capacity at its SYD1 facility in Sydney, taking the site to 100% contracted across its planned 88MW capacity as the company accelerates its Australian growth strategy and sells assets in the US. The agreement is with an unnamed global technology firm and […]
stories.content:
DigiCo Infrastructure REIT has signed a 15-year contract for 71MW of data centre capacity at its SYD1 facility in Sydney, taking the site to 100% contracted across its planned 88MW capacity as the company accelerates its Australian growth strategy and sells assets in the US.

The agreement is with an unnamed global technology firm and includes investment-grade credit support. The contract is subject to customary conditions and approvals. The deal covers 71MW of SYD1’s total 88MW capacity, including 20MW of existing contracted capacity reallocated to the new customer. The remaining 17MW is leased to colocation customers, according to DigiCo.

The agreement increases the weighted average lease expiry of DigiCo’s Australian portfolio from around three years to more than 10 years, on a pro forma basis assuming the full 88MW is income-producing. Weighted average annual escalations are approximately 3%, reflecting fixed escalators and CPI-linked reviews assuming CPI of 3%.

Simon Mitchell, DigiCo’s co-head and chief financial officer, said the contract marked a key milestone for the company. “When we acquired SYD1, our business plan was to fully lease and develop the site to 88MW over five years, and we now expect to reach that milestone well ahead of our original plan,” he said.

### Expansion moves ahead

DigiCo has also executed a fixed-price, lump-sum design and construction contract for the next 52MW of SYD1 capacity. Shape Australia has been appointed head contractor, while Laing O’Rourke will continue as the project’s integrated delivery partner.

The expansion will reuse an established data centre site with approved grid capacity, water access and state significant development approval. Construction is to be staged around customer requirements, with the first 10MW expected to be energised and generating income in late Q4 FY27, followed by the remaining capacity progressively through FY28.

DigiCo said the SYD1 expansion remains fully funded through existing liquidity, available debt facilities and proceeds from US asset sales, without requiring new equity.

The combined capex estimate for the SYD1 expansion and the 15MW brownfield expansion at its ADL1 facility in Adelaide, which DigiCo says is underpinned by advanced customer discussions, is AU$1.2 billion over FY27 and FY28. DigiCo expects the two projects, once fully operational and stabilised, to support approximately AU$250 million in annual Australian platform EBITDA.

### US asset sales fund domestic growth

The contract comes as DigiCo reshapes its portfolio around Australia, describing the domestic market as supply-constrained and prioritising capital deployment into its Australian data centre platform.

In its FY26 annual report, DigiCo said it was moving from portfolio assembly to portfolio optimisation, using asset sales to strengthen its balance sheet and fund higher-priority development opportunities.

The company completed the sale of its Chicago data centre, CHI1, on 10 September for US$750 million. It has also agreed to a conditional sale of its LAX1 and LAX2 sites in Los Angeles, at a price broadly in line with their acquisition cost. Completion of the Los Angeles transaction was expected in the first half of FY27, subject to customary closing conditions.

DigiCo has retained its Kansas City and Dallas-Fort Worth data centres, agreeing to extend both lease terms to 10 years expiring in 2036. The planned US divestments are expected to reduce gearing from 39% at the end of FY26 to a pro forma 18%, subject to transaction costs and completion adjustments, and increase available liquidity to approximately AU$1.2 billion.

DigiCo reported underlying EBITDA of AU$126.6 million for FY26, alongside a statutory loss after tax of AU$100.8 million. It has reaffirmed FY27 underlying EBITDA guidance of AU$120 million to AU$125 million, including two months of contribution from CHI1 before its sale.

The company’s Australian expansion plans are centred on increasing capacity at existing sites, with brownfield development prioritised while it evaluates greenfield opportunities with access to low-cost renewable power.

Mitchell said the 15-year agreement provides long-term earnings visibility. Ralph Goninan, DigiCo’s co-head and chief development officer, said the design and construct contract supports staged delivery aligned to the customer’s capacity requirements, with works carried out inside an operating data centre and uptime maintained for existing customers.

stories.title: IREN plans 900MW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga
stories.summary: AI cloud provider IREN has outlined plans for a 900MW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga, NSW, with a proposed investment of more than AU$10 billion, according to reports, and a target of initial energisation in 2029. The Nasdaq-listed company announced the proposed Redbank project to the local community, saying it remained in an early […]
stories.content:
AI cloud provider IREN has outlined plans for a 900MW data centre campus near Wagga Wagga, NSW, with a proposed investment of more than AU$10 billion, according to reports, and a target of initial energisation in 2029.

The Nasdaq-listed company announced the proposed Redbank project to the local community, saying it remained in an early assessment phase and was not included in its announced 5GW secured-power portfolio.

IREN said it was working towards a grid connection and reportedly planned to lodge a scoping report with the NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure at the end of October. The report is the first step in the state’s planning process and will help establish the requirements for a detailed environmental impact statement.

The campus would be developed in stages over six to eight years, according to reporting by The Daily Advertiser. IREN executive director Lindsay Ward told the newspaper the company was attracted to the site because it was not on prime agricultural land, was near electricity infrastructure and had access to local support services.

### Wagga cluster forming

Redbank is planned for the Gregadoo area on Wagga Wagga’s southern outskirts, west of the Gregadoo Waste Management Centre. It would be close to CDC Data Centres’ separately proposed 1.4GW campus off Ashfords Road, putting two large-scale data centre proposals in the same regional cluster.

Together, the projects represent up to 2.3GW of proposed capacity, although neither figure should be treated as secured demand or approved development. CDC has lodged its scoping report and is awaiting the next stage of assessment.

IREN is targeting more than 500 construction jobs and more than 200 ongoing full-time roles at Redbank. Ward told The Daily Advertiser the company would build a workers’ camp on the project site to avoid adding pressure on Wagga Wagga’s housing. IREN’s community information page speaks more broadly, saying the company is investigating several options, including an accommodation camp for the construction workforce on site and new housing for operational staff.

IREN has also forecast more than AU$200 million in payments to Wagga Wagga City Council over 30 years, including community benefits, local infrastructure and council rates.

The company says it intends to connect to the existing high-voltage network and fund its own connection. It also plans to contract new generation and storage to cover the campus’s electricity requirements. However, the project is not part of IREN’s announced secured-power portfolio, and the company has not announced a final grid connection agreement for Redbank.

The site is expected to use closed-loop cooling. According to IREN, filling the system is expected to require about three megalitres of water every six months during construction, with annual top-ups below one percent of the system’s total capacity once filled.

Redbank would be IREN’s second Australian data centre campus after its planned 800MW Bundey development in South Australia, for which it announced a transmission connection agreement in June. The company operates data centres in Canada and the United States and supplies AI computing capacity to customers including Microsoft and Nvidia.

IREN said it will hold community drop-in sessions in the city on 4 and 5 November, with further project details expected to emerge through the planning process.

stories.title: OpenAI again shakes up data center leadership, with xAI exec Uday Ruddarraju to lead and Sachin Katti to leave
stories.summary: After switching out the Stargate team earlier this year
stories.content:
OpenAI has appointed Uday Ruddarraju to lead its infrastructure and compute businesses, running its Stargate and other data center efforts.

Ruddarraju joined OpenAI last July as head of compute and infrastructure, and was named OpenAI's CTO of Compute this July. His latest promotion was first reported by Bloomberg.

The former xAI exec, who served as head of infrastructure engineering at the SpaceX business, replaces Sachin Katti.

Katti joined from Intel in November 2025, and took over the Stargate data center effort this March. OpenAI data center heads Peter Hoeschele, Keith Heyde, Shamez Hemani, and Chris Malone left the company following Katti's promotion.

Under Katti, OpenAI expanded its cloud partnerships as in-house data center projects remain slow to come online. The company projects spending about $750 billion on computing power through 2030, up from an earlier estimate of roughly $600bn.

Katti is expected to remain as an adviser.

Ruddarraju's data center team has been increasingly bolstered by fellow former xAI (now SpaceXAI, soon SpaceXSI) employees, including OpenAI's head of data center build and delivery Brent Mayo.

Also of note are xAI's site lead Aakash Verma, data center infrastructure staffer Amin Golnabi, project manager Andrej Sulek, and construction project manager Johnathan Henley, who have all joined OpenAI.

This month, the former lead commissioning engineer at xAI, Michael Roberson, joined OpenAI's infrastructure division.

stories.summary: Project targeting 2028/2029 go live date
stories.content:
Plans have been filed for a new data center campus outside Augusta, Richmond.

A development of regional impact application has been filed by 3 G Investments, LLC with the Georgia State Department of Community Affairs for the Nixon Technology Center.

Located at 1538 and 1550 Four H Club Road and 3806 Mike Padgett Highway in Richmond County, the project is set to total 3.34 million sq ft (310,296 sqm) of data center space across 388 acres. The project could come online in 2028/2029.

The proposed site is largely vacant land adjacent to Augusta Regional Airport, just outside Augusta and some 150 miles (241 kms) east of Atlanta. Full details of the development haven’t been shared.

The property owner is listed as the Nixon Trusts, represented by Augusta real estate law firm Trotter Jones.

It's unclear if any data center developers or end users are involved in the project at this point.

SGPB Holdings, LLLP, on behalf of The Nixon Trusts, last year requested to rezone 100 acres at 1550 Four H Club Road from agricultural to heavy industrial to develop a manufacturing warehouse. The request was granted by the Augusta planning commission in November.

Google, QTS, and Cloverleaf have a data center presence around Augusta.

Atlanta and its surrounding areas have traditionally been a Tier 2 market, but increased demand for data centers has resulted in a surge of data center proposals.

DRI applications for more than a dozen campuses, totaling tens of millions of square feet across dozens of buildings, have been filed over the last couple of years. While many are in Atlanta’s traditional data center heartland around Fulton County, applications have been filed for projects across the Peach State.

It said 16 of the projects are in Johor, 10 in Selangor and one in Negeri Sembilan, adding that one of the data centres has begun operating, while the rest are still under construction.

The ministry said this in a written reply to a question from Datuk Dr Ahmad Yunus Hairi (PN-Kuala Langat) on the number of data centres approved under the DCTF by state and their economic spillover benefits for local communities.

It said the projects are expected to create 4,053 jobs, including 3,523 high-skilled positions in the fields of electrical and mechanical engineering, networking, cybersecurity, as well as data centre operations and maintenance.

Malaysians are expected to fill 89.21% of the high-skilled positions.

“Projects approved under the DCTF are subject to a minimum local content requirement of 30%, with implementation and compliance monitored by the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida) through project implementation reports that must be submitted every six months.

“To strengthen the technology and skills transfers, Talent Corporation Malaysia is developing a data centre facilities management programme to train local participants in skills related to data centre operations and maintenance,” the ministry said.

stories.title: IURC approves AES Indiana plan for $1.3bn solar, storage, and transmission project for Google data center in Monrovia
stories.summary: Google is expected to pay for all the costs associated with the project
stories.content:
The Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) has approved plans filed by state utility AES Indiana to construct a solar + battery project and transmission line set to power a Google data center in Monrovia.

Under the agreement, Google will pay all costs associated with the project. The IURC said that the proposed project was approved as it met the requirements set out under a law passed in 2025 that requires all large load data centers to cover at minimum 80 percent of the costs associated with the generation and transmission infrastructure needed to power it.

The project comprises two standalone Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), with a capacity of 200MW and 130MW respectively. It also comprises a hybrid solar + battery project with 130MW of solar power paired with a 130MW BESS. The project also includes a 10-mile (16km) 345kV power line connecting the project to an on-site substation near the data center, which includes a planned 1,200MW substation.

AES has said that the project will cost approximately $1.3 billion to construct.

Commissioner Joby Jerrells said AES Indiana had testified that Google would pay for at least 100 percent of the costs under the requirement.

"Not only does this agreement satisfy the statutory requirement, it exceeds it substantially," Jerrells said.

According to local reporting, AES US Utilities CEO Gustavo Garaviglia said that Google will pay $32.3 million for direct connection facilities, while $73.8m in network upgrades will be included in AES's transmission rate base.

The contract between AES and Google will last at least 15 years, and includes several provisions to prevent cost shifting onto regular ratepayers if Google decides either to scale back or drop the project.

News that Google was behind the Monrovia development first emerged last October. Earlier that year, an application for the project was submitted for land located in Morgan Township, east of Monrovia, between Keller Hill Road, North Antioch Road, Indiana 42, and West Union Church Road. It encompasses 18 parcels owned by ten different entities.

Of the five buildings proposed, four seem to be large data centers, and the fifth is a smaller building east of the electrical transmission line.

Google is also developing a campus in Fort Wayne, Indiana, having purchased 900 acres and committed around $2bn to the project in 2024. This was expanded in September 2025.

stories.title: Iren targets 900MW data center campus in Wagga Wagga, Australia
stories.summary: Company aiming for 2029 grid connection
stories.content:
Data center and cloud firm Iren has outlined plans for a new data center campus in Australia.

Iren this week announced plans for Redbank, a proposed data center campus near Wagga Wagga in regional New South Wales.

The company said the 900MW campus is in the early assessment phase and the firm is working toward a grid connection starting in 2029. The campus could see more than AU$10 billion (US$7bn) invested.

Wagga Wagga is a city in the Riverina region of New South Wales, some 455km (283 miles) southwest of Sydney and more than 230km (143 miles) west of Canberra.

According to a dedicated project website, the proposed campus site sits west of the Gregadoo Waste Management Centre, near Wagga Wagga on land that hosts existing transmission infrastructure.

Site renderings suggest at least four buildings of varying sizes and an on-site substation.

The grid-connected project would see Iren fund transmission costs and contract new renewable energy and storage to cover its needs. The campus would also have a closed-loop cooling system to reduce water use.

Iren noted the project is not included in its previously announced 5GW secured-power portfolio.

“Redbank has the potential to create local jobs and economic stimulus as well as community benefits for the Wagga Wagga area,” the company said.

Leading Edge DC, an Australian Edge data center firm, has a small facility in Wagga Wagga. CDC is also looking to develop in Wagga Wagga, with plans for a gigawatt-scale campus.

Founded in 2019, Iren has crypto and AI sites located across Canada and the US. It has some 23,000 GPUs in its fleet, with Microsoft as a major customer. The company has data center sites live and in development across Texas (Childress, Sweetwater), Oklahoma (Kiowa), and British Columbia in Canada (Mackenzie, Prince George, and Canal Flats). It recently acquired Spanish data center developer Nostrum, marking its entry into Europe.

Iren is also targeting an 800MW campus in Bundey, South Australia. Announced in June, a grid connection is expected around 2028.

The company alluded to a potential expansion to Australia earlier this year when it reported its financial results. CEO Roberts said at the time that the opportunity down under was “as significant as anywhere in our portfolio.”

stories.title: Soluna files to build 112MW data center building in Willacy, Texas
stories.summary: Will span a single building totaling 471,884 sq ft
stories.content:
AI and cryptocurrency data center developer Soluna has filed to build a 112MW data center in Willacy, Texas.

According to a filing with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, the data center, dubbed Project Kati II, will span a single building totaling 471,884 sq ft (43,839 sqm). The filing stipulates that the data center will cost approximately $471.8 million to construct and will be privately funded on private land for private use. The filing did not provide a timeline for the data center's construction.

News of the project first arose in January, with the data center expected to be constructed in partnership with Metrobloks. Soluna subsequently confirmed that a definitive joint venture agreement was signed on June 3.

The project is seemingly an extension of the company’s Project Kati I data center. The data center has a planned capacity of 166MW at full buildout, with 83MW as part of its first phase. Initial energization began on February 9, 2026, and Phase I was completed in September 2026. The data center is connected to the 273 MW Las Majadas Wind Project, which serves the project behind the meter.

Soluna is a cryptocurrency mining firm that utilizes renewable energy projects as its primary power source. The company has a total operational capacity of 192MW and 11 data center sites in various stages of development.

This includes the 187MW Project Rosa site in Texas; the 50MW Dorothy I A and B, as well as 48MW Dorothy II, again in Texas; Project Sophie, a 25MW data center in Kentucky; and the 2MW Grace site in Texas.

In August, the firm acquired a 397-acre plot in Briscoe County, Texas, where it plans to build its Project Dorothy III data center. The campus is expected to have a capacity of up to 300MW and will sit adjacent to two other projects on the site, Dorothy I and II. The data center is expected to be powered by renewable energy, sitting next to the 150MW Briscoe onshore wind farm, which the company purchased in April.

stories.title: Submer partners with BSNL for data center development in India
stories.summary: Companies look to use BSNL sites for data center development
stories.content:
Data center firm Submer and Indian telco Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited (BSNL) are partnering to potentially develop data centers across India.

Submer India Private Limited (Submer) and BSNL Tower Corporation Limited (BTCL), a wholly owned subsidiary of BSNL, signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) this week at the India Mobile Congress 2026 to “explore the development of sovereign, AI-ready data center infrastructure across India.”

The companies said they will jointly assess opportunities around GPU-as-a-Service, sovereign AI cloud infrastructure, Edge and micro data centers, and larger-scale data center projects of up to 20MW.

The firms will also evaluate the suitability of BSNL's existing premises and data center facilities for transformation into distributed Edge infrastructure.

Shri Robert Jerard Ravi, BSNL chairman and MD, said: “This MoU marks an important step in evaluating how BSNL’s nationwide infrastructure and connectivity footprint can support sovereign AI capabilities. Our collaboration with Submer will help us explore an infrastructure model designed around India’s long-term digital priorities.”

Founded in 2000, BSNL is the fourth-largest mobile operator in India and also offers fiber services across the country.

The company currently has nine data centers across India in New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Faridabad, Alappuzha, Bangalore, Jaipur, Mumbai, Hyderabad, and Ludhiana. As well as a portfolio of telephone exchanges powering its legacy copper network, the company operates thousands of cell towers across the country for its 4G and 5G networks.

“India has the talent, demand, and digital reach to become a global AI infrastructure leader. The next step is to build the physical capacity that turns that ambition into deployable compute,” added Anupam Shrivastava, Submer India head. “Together with BTCL, we are bringing infrastructure, network reach, and engineering expertise into one model. Our goal is clear: make sovereign AI capacity available where it is needed, from strategic Edge locations to large-scale AI data centers.”

Spanish firm Submer was founded in 2015. Originally focused on immersion cooling, the company has expanded into data center development and providing AI cloud services through its Rubix Data Centers and Radian Arc units. It also offers modular data center infrastructure through its new Corenix business.

Submer has made multiple moves in India this year. The firm’s AI cloud subsidiary, Radian Arc, is set to deploy its GPU-as-a-Service offering within GTPL Broadband's network and in TeleIndia Datacentre (Datasamudra) data centers in the country. Submer is also set to deploy 1GW of liquid-cooled AI data centers in Madhya Pradesh. The company has also partnered with Indian real estate developer Anant Raj to develop data centers in India.

stories.title: Digi Power X secures $200m in debt financing for Alabama data center project
stories.summary: Will support the development of a 40MW data center in Columbiana, Alabama
stories.content:
Data center and energy infrastructure developer Digi Power X has secured a $200 million commitment in debt financing for its data center project in Alabama.

The funding has been syndicated by Goldman Sachs and is being provided by an unnamed "major lending institution."

Digi Power X will use the financing to support the development of its 40MW data center project in Columbiana, Alabama.

The data center is being developed in two phases: phase one with 15MW of IT load, and phase two to deliver 25MW incrementally for a total IT capacity of 40MW. The phases will be delivered by the end of 2026 and the end of Q1 2027, respectively. According to Digi Power X, the project remains on track.

Wafer-scale chip company and cloud provider Cerebras signed on for the full capacity at the site in May of this year.

At the time of writing, Digi Power X holds approximately $135 million in cash and has invested approximately $153 million in capital expenditures in 2026.

Formerly known as Digihost, Digi Power X was previously focused on mining cryptocurrencies and placing mining hardware at power plants for itself and other companies. As with many other crypto firms, the company is pivoting to host AI hardware amid a capacity crunch, and in 2025 launched US Data Centers to focus on AI and HPC colocation.

Through US Data Centers, the company operates modular Arms 200 compute units, for which it has one deployment already up and running.

Digi Power owns and operates three data center sites across Columbiana, as well as Buffalo and North Tonawanda in New York, and has also acquired an office and laboratory facility in Silicon Valley to develop the technology and operational intelligence supporting its AI token factory strategy.

The company is aiming to transform its New York sites into AI data centers, though plans have been impacted by a local data center moratorium signed into law in June 2026.

stories.title: Microsoft acquires 600 acres of land for data center in Woodward, Iowa
stories.summary: Local residents raise concerns
stories.content:
Microsoft has acquired 600 acres of land outside Des Moines, Iowa, for a potential data center campus.

As reported by the Des Moines Register, the land purchase in Woodward was revealed on October 12 during a meeting with local residents. The sale went through just four days prior, on October 8.

The land lies between Highway 141 and Seminole Avenue. Woodward is located around 30 miles northwest of Des Moines in Dallas County.

While the land was acquired for a data center campus, plans remain largely undecided.

At least 300 local residents attended the meeting earlier this week, which was held after the council's regular meeting was canceled. During the meeting, residents asked Mayor Todd Folkerts if they got a vote on the project, to which Folkerts responded: "No." According to the Des Moines Register, one resident shouted: "You work for the people." One resident was forcibly removed from the meeting.

Microsoft's land development manager, Jackie Nickolaus, told residents: "We have not even begun to design the building, so we have no idea what mechanical systems will be going into the buildings." She estimated that it would take two to three years to design the campus before construction work would begin, and the first building would take around two years to complete.

Nickolaus added that the data center is expected to serve cloud computing and data storage workloads, not AI training workloads.

The property Microsoft purchased was rezoned from agricultural use to Eco Business Park District in June 2026, with the council waiving the usual additional readings of the ordinance.

The value of the land purchase agreement has not been shared, but another area of the Eco Business Park is offering 59 acres at $62,400 per acre. Should the Microsoft land be priced the same, this would put the transaction at around $37.4m.

Microsoft is known to be developing various projects in the Des Moines area. In 2024, the company purchased 111 acres for Project Ruthenium. Other Microsoft data center sites in the area in various stages of development and operation include Project Ginger West, Project Ginger East, as well as Project Mountain, and Project Alluvion.

Tract is also developing in the Des Moines area, having acquired 282 acres earlier this year.

stories.title: UK-based AI infrastructure firm Gorilla Technology Group to enter US market with proposed 6MW data center acquisition
stories.summary: Site has the potential to expand to 36MW
stories.content:
With an expected completion in late November 2026, Gorilla said the acquisition was the first step in an expansion strategy that will see the company secure 100MW of capacity over the next year and a half.

The existing facility is an operational and revenue-generating colocation facility with around 6MW of capacity, but Gorilla says there is a “pathway” to 36MW of total site power capacity. The company says it has already obtained written support from local utilities for another 30MW of power, with an 18-month delivery timetable.

The facility will continue with its current operations following the proposed acquisition. The location and current owner of the site were not named.

Gorilla said the site has “expansion potential,” with expansion happening in phases, focusing on customer requirements and next-generation GPU systems.

Gorilla currently has several AI compute deployments in data centers across the Asia-Pacific region, including India, Thailand, and Indonesia.

“This is a defining step in Gorilla’s expansion into the US,” said Jay Chandan, chairman and CEO of Gorilla. “We have spent considerable time evaluating how we enter this market, and we believe the right approach is to own and control the infrastructure that sits underneath the AI economy.”

“We are not entering the United States simply to acquire a building. We are establishing the first piece of what we aim to become a significant AI infrastructure business. The combination of power, infrastructure, connectivity and customer demand gives us the opportunity to build something considerably larger from this initial platform.

He added: “Our objective is to control more of the infrastructure stack supporting our customers. Owning the data-center platform gives us greater control over deployment timelines, power, cooling and operating economics. Combined with customer-led GPU deployment, we believe that creates a significantly stronger long-term business model.”

The deal is subject to due diligence, including infrastructure assessment, utility and power verification, property and lease review, site inspection, and preparation of the development programme for the facility.

stories.title: Indonesia forms national team to support data center development
stories.summary: Indonesia's Ministry of Industry plans to establish a national team to support data center development. This initiative aims to address the substantial water and electricity demands of these facilities.
stories.content:
Indonesia’s Ministry of Industry is setting up a national team to support data center development across the country.The team will include government institutions and the Indonesian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, according to Deputy Industry Minister Faisol Riza. He announced the initiative in Jakarta on Tuesday, as reported by Antara News.Data centers are crucial for industries and serve as catalysts for economic growth, Riza said. The team's formation follows feedback from other ministries, government agencies, and state-owned enterprises regarding the significant water and electricity requirements for data centers.This announcement comes after the suspension of work on BDx Data Centers’ 640 MW artificial intelligence (AI) data center project in Jatiluhur, West Java. West Java Governor Dedi Mulyadi ordered the halt because the project lacked an Environmental Impact Assessment and Building Approval Documents.BDx representatives informed the governor that the necessary permits were expected by early October. Construction on the data center had begun in September, with Building 1 planned to deliver 120 MW of IT capacity in phases.The first contracted phase was initially expected to be operational in early 2027, but this timeline could change due to the stoppage order. Riza stated he would coordinate with relevant stakeholders to address these issues.He added that discussions would involve the West Java government and several ministries and agencies, covering the Jatiluhur data center and similar projects elsewhere. Coordinating Minister for Infrastructure and Regional Development Agus Harimurti Yudhoyono emphasised on Monday that all data center projects must comply with environmental regulations.According to Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, the Indonesian data center market was valued at US$2.82 billion in 2025. It is projected to more than double to US$6.09 billion by 2031, positioning Indonesia as a major data center hub and an alternative to Singapore.

stories.title: Adani Enterprises and Jabil sign MoU for 50:50 data center hardware JV
stories.summary: Adani Enterprises Limited, the flagship company of the Adani Group, and Jabil Inc., a global engineering, supply chain and manufacturing company, have signed a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) setting out the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble AI and data center equipment in India. In a press release, the […]
stories.content:
Adani Enterprises Limited, the flagship company of the Adani Group, and Jabil Inc., a global engineering, supply chain and manufacturing company, have signed a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) setting out the framework for a proposed 50:50 joint venture to manufacture and assemble AI and data center equipment in India.

In a press release, the companies revealed that the JV would manufacture and assemble AI racks, servers, storage and networking equipment used in data centers. The racks would house high-performance computing systems for AI applications and other digital services.

The portfolio would also include equipment required to power and cool these systems, including power distribution units, liquid-cooling systems and transformers. The venture is expected to have multi-gigawatt AI rack manufacturing capacity, supporting computing systems with a combined power capacity of several gigawatts. It would also provide installation and commissioning services.

“The AI revolution will demand far more than just breakthroughs in algorithms. It will require an entire new industrial architecture where energy, hyperscale infrastructure, advanced computing and precision manufacturing converge to power the intelligence economy,” said Gautam Adani, Chairman, Adani Group. “Our proposed joint venture with Jabil marks a strategic step towards this future, combining Jabil’s world-class engineering and manufacturing capabilities with Adani’s integrated strengths in energy, infrastructure and data centers to help build the physical backbone of the global AI economy.”

Mike Dastoor, Chief Executive Officer (CEO), Jabil Inc., said, “The signing of this MoU is the next step forward in our shared efforts to establish a scaled AI infrastructure manufacturing platform in India, a market we believe will become increasingly important for both domestic and global AI infrastructure demand.”

The MoU follows the June 2026 announcement of Adani Group and Jabil’s intent to establish a strategic alliance to develop an AI and data center infrastructure manufacturing ecosystem in India. The venture would provide a manufacturing base in India to serve domestic demand and support exports. The companies estimate the global market opportunity at more than US$ 3 trillion over the next seven years, driven by investment in AI computing.

For Jabil, which reported US$ 36 billion in revenue in fiscal year 2026, the venture would expand its engineering and manufacturing footprint in India’s data center market.

The venture is aligned with Adani Group’s $100 billion commitment to develop 5 GW of green-energy-powered, hyperscale AI-ready data centers by 2035. The proposed venture would add hardware manufacturing to the Group’s presence across infrastructure, energy, logistics and data centers.

The proposed joint venture remains subject to execution of definitive agreements and satisfaction of applicable approvals and customary conditions.

stories.title: Singapore’s PDG seeking US$1.2 billion loan for Johor data centre: source
stories.summary: HSBC Singapore, Maybank, UOB said to be among mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for three-year deal

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
HSBC Singapore, Maybank, UOB said to be among mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for three-year deal

\[SINGAPORE\] Asian data-centre operator Princeton Digital Group (PDG) is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion to fund its Malaysia build-out, according to a person familiar with the matter, as the debt binge to finance artificial-intelligence infrastructure continues.

HSBC’s Singapore branch, Maybank, OCBC Bank (Malaysia), Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore), and UOB are the mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for the three-year loan deal, said the person, asking not to be identified discussing private information.

Proceeds from the loan to be taken by the company’s subsidiary, Princeton Digital Group Labuan Alpha, will be used to fund a 198.8-megawatt data-centre campus project in Johor, Malaysia, and to refinance existing debt, the person said.

StanChart declined to comment. Representatives for PDG, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC Malaysia and UOB did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Data-centre companies across the world have been taking on debt as they seek to raise capital to meet growing AI demand. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt.

But there are signs that global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations as evidenced by the collapse of Nvidia Corp-backed data centre operator Firmus Grid’s initial public offering last week.

Data-centre firm AirTrunk, which counts Blackstone as a key investor, was reported to delay its planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until next year as higher interest rates and market volatility temper investor demand.

Headquartered in Singapore, PDG’s top shareholder is Warburg Pincus and other investors include Stonepeak Partners, Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala Investment and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board.

The firm, founded in 2018, operates more than 1.8 gigawatts of data-centre capacity across Asia including in China, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, according to its website.

PDG has been on a borrowing spree as it seeks to expand across Asia. In May, the firm said that it raised around US$856 million for its data-centre build-out in Indonesia.

Earlier in the year, the company said that it was targeting to raise US$5 billion in debt to support regional expansion plans. BLOOMBERG
